 Her Husband Claimed Social Security at 62 to Protect Their $300,000 Nest Egg. Widows Fare Worse When Husbands Claim Early, and Her Survivor Check Could Be $1,245 a Month Smaller Than if He’d Waited Until 70
 By Gerelyn Terzo 
 Published November 15, 2026, 5:32am ET · 4 min read 
 The Full Benefits Desk desk. Editor: Gerelyn Terzo .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 A husband's early claiming at 62 locks in a reduced benefit that caps his widow's survivor check, leaving her about $1,245 less monthly than if he waited until 70.
 Over a 15-year widowhood, that gap totals about $224,000, nearly the $300,000 nest egg the early claim aimed to protect.
 Couples should compare survivor benefits at each claiming age, since delay pays off most for the higher earner and bridging with savings buys an inflation-adjusted pension.

 A couple at 62 with $300,000 saved often faces the same worry. If he holds off for a bigger Social Security check, they have to spend down the nest egg in the meantime, so he files early, the savings stay intact, and the decision feels reasonable. What rarely comes up at the kitchen table is this. His claiming age also sets the size of the check his wife may live on for years after he is gone.
 Couples are starting to ask about this. A woman recently asked a personal finance podcast. She had just turned 60 and wanted to know whether her husband could collect her larger benefit if she died before claiming it, since the two of them hoped to hold off until 70. The answer was yes, because a survivor benefit follows the deceased spouse’s record whether or not that spouse ever filed. That same rule works against a widow when the record was locked in early.
 His Claiming Age Silently Becomes Her Paycheck
 Picture a husband whose full benefit at 67 would be $3,000 a month. Claiming at 62 cuts it by 30%, according to the Social Security Administration, to $2,100.
 Waiting past 67 adds 8% [ 1 ] for each year of delay until 70, for $3,720.
 When he dies, she keeps one check. Social Security pays her the larger of her own benefit or what she receives from his record, never both added together. If he claimed early, a rule called the widow’s limit caps her survivor check at the larger of his reduced benefit or 82 1/2% [ 2 ] of his full amount, assuming she has reached her full age. In this example, that comes to $2,475.
 Had he holds off until 70, she would step into the full $3,720 instead. That gap of $1,245 a month adds up to $14,940 a year.
 Over a 15-year widowhood, it totals $224,100, a sum nearing the very nest egg the early claim was meant to protect.
 Annual inflation adjustments keep that gap in place for life. The 2026 raise was 2.8% [ 3 ] , applied to whatever base she starts with, so a smaller check stays proportionally smaller. The 2027 increase is 3.6%. Meanwhile, the CPI-W, which the Fed uses in its calculation to determine the cost-of-living bump, has climbed 3.9% in the 12 months through September.
 Spending Savings Now to Buy Her a Bigger Check Later
 The concern about draining $300,000 is legitimate.
 Replacing his $2,100 check from savings until 67 would take about $126,000 before any investment growth. Bridging all the way to 70 would take more, which is why many couples settle somewhere in between.
 Even reaching 67 raises her check. Her survivor benefit jumps from $2,475 to $3,000, an extra $525 a month. Think of those early withdrawals as buying an inflation-adjusted pension that pays whichever spouse lives longer, something difficult to match with savings sitting in an IRA.
 Taxes shift after a death, too. A widow generally moves to single filing, and the income level where Social Security starts becoming taxable drops from $32,000 for married couples to $25,000. Traditional IRAs and 401(k)s also carry required minimum distributions (RMDs) during the owner’s lifetime, which stack on top of her survivor check. Spending down some of those pre-tax dollars in the bridge years can reduce those future withdrawals, so delaying his claim can help on both fronts.
 What to Weigh Before Either of You Files
 Start with one question: who is likely to live longer? If he is the higher earner and she is younger or in better health, his claiming age is really a decision about her income in her 80s and 90s. Delay pays off most for the bigger earner, even if the lower earner claims early to ease cash flow.
 The mistake toughest to undo is filing early without running the survivor math. Once he has collected for a while, his reduced check becomes the anchor for her widow’s limit, and the escape options are narrow. Pull both earnings records from your online Social Security accounts and compare his benefit at 62, 67, and 70 against what she would receive as a widow at each age.
 No two households have identical profiles. Their ages, health histories, savings mix, and even small details like a modest pension or a few years’ age difference can tip the answer. An afternoon spent with your real numbers, alone or with a fee-only planner, may matter more to her future than any investment decision you make this decade.
